query: Which material can be used for ductility, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Introducing low levels of nickel into a low-carbon steel matrix will increase its ductility compared to undoped low-carbon steel.
generation.intervention: Alloying the steel with a small nickel content (around 2–4 wt%).
generation.conditions: Standard steelmaking with controlled cooling from 900–1200°C after alloying.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced stacking fault energy that enables more uniform slip during deformation.
generation.mechanism: Nickel modifies the crystal lattice and increases dislocation mobility, resulting in improved plastic deformation capacity.
generation.predicted_outcome: An appreciable increase in elongation before fracture (e.g., up to 20% higher) compared to undoped low-carbon steel.
generation.baseline: Undoped low-carbon steel, which generally exhibits moderate ductility under similar thermal processing.
generation.boundary: If nickel content exceeds around 5 wt%, potential grain boundary effects could limit further ductility improvements.
generation.uncertainty: Exact ductility enhancements depend on specific alloy composition and thermal history, so the improvement range is not precisely known.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare steel samples with varying Ni levels (0–6 wt%), subject them to the same thermal processing, then compare tensile properties.
measurements: Microstructural characterization (e.g., grain size, dislocation structures)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If tensile tests do not show a systematic improvement in elongation with nickel additions, or if the ductility does not exceed that of the baseline at these doping levels, the hypothesis is falsified.
